title: Java
intro: This term you learn Java, the strict and powerful language behind Android apps and bank systems. Step by step you will build a real inventory manager for a Nigerian provision shop.
termProject: Mama Tunde's Provision Shop Inventory Manager: a Java program with Product classes, promo and perishable rules, friendly error handling for wrong input and out-of-stock orders, and a stock file it saves at closing and reads every morning to flag what to restock.

weeks.title: Hello Java, Hello Mama Tunde's Shop
weeks.goal: I can write, compile and run a Java program that stores shop details in variables and prints them.
weeks.learn: Java is a strict but powerful language used in Android apps, banks and big company systems. Every Java program lives inside a class, and it starts running from the main method. Every statement ends with a semicolon, and you must say what type a variable is before you use it. Java is like a careful bank teller: everything must be filled in correctly on the slip before she will accept it.

research.q: Ask a provision shop owner (or your parent): what are the three items you sell the most, and how much is each?
research.tip: Write the item names and prices. They become the variables in your first Java program.

build.task: Write a Java program that prints a shop name, how many tins of milk are in stock, and their total value.
steps: Save the code in a file named exactly ShopHello.java
Compile it: javac ShopHello.java
Run it: java ShopHello
Change the values to an item from your research and run again

check.q: Where does a Java program start running?
What must end almost every Java statement?
If the class is called ShopHello, the file must be named...

weeks.say: Java starts in main, every statement ends with a semicolon, and every variable must have a type, like a well-filled bank slip.

trainer.open: You already speak Python and JavaScript. Today you meet Java - the strict bank teller of programming languages.
plan: Show a bank deposit slip and point at the boxes that must be filled correctly
Type ShopHello together; show javac then java
Pairs swap in the items from their research and run
Pairs read out their shop's total stock value
lookfor: Names the file to match the class exactly
Explains the difference between javac (compile) and java (run)
Changes the variables without breaking the semicolons
fix: Gets 'class ShopHello is public, should be declared in a file named ShopHello.java'
Java is strict: the file name and the public class name must be the same, capital letters too
Forgets a semicolon and sees '; expected'
Read the line number in the error - Java tells you where the slip is incomplete

weeks.title: Data Types: Cartons, Kilos and True/False
weeks.goal: I can choose the right Java data type for each kind of shop information and convert between them.
weeks.learn: Java has a box type for every kind of data: int for whole numbers (cartons), double for numbers with a point (kilos of sugar), char for one letter, boolean for true or false, and String for text. final makes a value that can never change. Casting with (int) chops off the decimals, like a trader who rounds down N2,450.70 to N2,450. Choosing the right type is like choosing the right container at the market: you do not carry palm oil in a basket.

research.q: Ask a trader: which things do you count in whole numbers, and which do you measure with scales or cups?
research.tip: Sort their answers into 'whole' (int) and 'measured' (double). That is exactly how Java thinks about numbers.

build.task: Use int, double, char, boolean, String and final for a noodles stock record and convert a double to an int.
steps: Save as ShopTypes.java
Compile and run it
Change 3.0 to 3 and run again - what changes?
Add one boolean of your own, like isNepaOn

check.q: Which type should hold 2.5 kg of sugar?
What does (int) 93.7 give you?
Which type can only be true or false?

weeks.say: I choose the right Java box for each kind of data - int for cartons, double for kilos, boolean for yes or no.

trainer.open: You do not carry palm oil in a basket. Java also wants the right container for every kind of data.
plan: Show a basket, a bottle and a bag - which holds what? Link to types
Walk through each line of ShopTypes
Pairs run, then change 3.0 to 3 to see integer division
Each learner adds one variable from their research with the correct type
props: A basket, a bottle and a small bag
lookfor: Picks int vs double correctly for their own examples
Explains why pieces / 3 loses the decimals
Uses single quotes for char and double quotes for String
fix: Writes int price = 450.50; and gets 'possible lossy conversion'
450.50 has a point - use double, or cast on purpose with (int) if you really want to chop it
Tries to change a final value
final means locked - like a fixed government price. Remove final only if it truly needs to change

weeks.title: Rules and Repeats: The Restock Checker
weeks.goal: I can use if/else if/else and for and while loops in Java to check every item and warn when stock is low.
weeks.learn: An if statement is a rule: if stock is zero, shout 'buy today!'. A for loop repeats the check for every item on the shelf, and a while loop keeps going until something changes, like bread running out. Java uses the same ideas as Python and JavaScript, but with curly braces { } and round brackets around every condition. It is like the shop girl's evening routine: check every shelf, and for each one decide - full, low, or finished.

research.q: Ask a shop owner: at what number of items left do you decide to restock? Is it the same for every item?
research.tip: Write the item and its restock number. Real restock rules make your if-statements meaningful.

build.task: Loop through four items, print FINISHED, LOW or OKAY for each, then count down bread sales day by day.
steps: Save as Restock.java, compile and run
Change the stock numbers to test each rule
Change 5 to the restock number from your research
Make the while loop sell 4 loaves a day instead of 6

check.q: In Java, which sign checks if two numbers are equal?
Which loop is best when you know you must check every item in an array?
What does Math.max(bread, 0) stop from happening?
opts: Printing a negative number of loaves

weeks.say: My for loop checks every shelf and my if-rules decide full, low or finished, just like the shop girl's evening routine.

trainer.open: Every evening someone in the shop walks round every shelf. Today Java does that walk for us.
plan: Act it out: one learner 'walks the shelves' calling out OKAY, LOW, FINISHED
Compare Java's if and for with Python's on the board
Pairs run Restock and test each rule
Share their research restock numbers and edit the rule
props: Four empty provision containers with number cards
lookfor: Explains each branch of the if/else if/else
Changes the loop or rule numbers correctly
Knows = stores a value and == compares
fix: Writes if (stock[i] = 0)
One = puts a value in the box; two == asks a question. Java wants a question here
Uses i <= items.length and gets ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Arrays start at 0, so the last index is length - 1. Use < not <=

weeks.title: Classes and Objects: Every Product Has a Card
weeks.goal: I can design a Product class, make objects from it, and use inheritance so a Drink gets everything a Product has.
weeks.learn: A class is a blueprint, and an object is a real thing made from it. Our Product class says every product has a name, price and quantity, and can work out its stock value. A Drink extends Product, so it inherits all of that and adds one extra thing: whether it is chilled. It is like a tailor's pattern: one pattern for a shirt, and a special version with an extra pocket.

research.q: Ask a shop owner: what details do you need to know about every product? Is there any item that needs extra details?
research.tip: List the details. Shared details go in the Product class; extra details go in a child class like Drink.

build.task: Create a Product class and a Drink class that extends it, then print the stock value of rice and zobo.
steps: Save everything in one file named Shop.java
Compile and run it
Make a new Product from your research list
Add a field like 'brand' to Product and see Drink get it too

check.q: What is the difference between a class and an object?
opts: A class is the blueprint, an object is a real thing made from it

check.q: What does 'Drink extends Product' mean?
opts: Drink gets everything Product has and can add more

check.q: What does super(name, price, qty) do?
opts: Calls the Product constructor to fill the shared details

weeks.say: A class is a pattern and objects are real products made from it; Drink inherits from Product like a shirt with an extra pocket.

trainer.open: A tailor does not draw a new pattern for every customer. Java classes work the same way.
plan: Show a paper pattern (or drawing) and two 'garments' made from it
Build Product, then Drink, explaining extends and super
Pairs run Shop and add a product from their research
Each pair names one more child class a shop needs (e.g. Frozen)
props: A tailor's paper pattern or a drawing of one
lookfor: Explains class vs object with their own example
Uses extends and super correctly
Proposes a sensible new child class from research
fix: Forgets super(...) in the Drink constructor and gets a constructor error
The child must let the parent set up first - call super(name, price, qty) as the first line
Writes Product rice = Product(...) without new
new is how Java cuts real cloth from the pattern - always use new to make an object

weeks.title: Polymorphism: Same Call, Different Behaviour
weeks.goal: I can override a method in child classes so one loop calls label() and each product answers in its own way.
weeks.learn: Polymorphism means 'many forms': the same method name can do different things depending on the object. Each child class overrides label() with its own version, marked @Override. Then one loop over a Product array calls p.label(), and Java picks the right version for each object. It is like shouting 'Announce your price!' in the market: the bread seller, the zobo seller and the garri seller all answer, but each in their own way.

research.q: Ask a trader: how do you call out or advertise different goods? Is it the same for bread and for garri?
research.tip: Write two different 'calls'. Those are two different versions of the same method - polymorphism in real life.

build.task: Override label() in Drink and Bread, then print every item on a mixed shelf with one loop.
steps: Save as Shelf.java, compile and run
Notice the loop has no if-statements but each label is different
Add a Garri class with its own label()
Put a Garri object on the shelf and run again

check.q: What does polymorphism mean?
opts: Many forms - the same call behaves differently for different objects

check.q: What does @Override tell Java?
opts: This method replaces the parent's version

check.q: Why can the shelf array hold Drink and Bread objects?
opts: Because Drink and Bread are kinds of Product

weeks.say: With polymorphism, one call to label() makes every product answer in its own way, like sellers calling out in the market.

trainer.open: In the market, everyone is selling, but nobody advertises bread the same way as garri. Today Java learns that trick.
plan: Role-play: trainer shouts 'Announce!' and three learners answer as different sellers
Show how @Override replaces label() in each child
Pairs run Shelf and add a Garri class
Ask: where would if-statements have been needed without polymorphism?
props: Three seller name cards (bread, zobo, garri)
lookfor: Adds a new child class with its own label() correctly
Explains why the loop needs no if-statements
Uses @Override in the right place
fix: Spells the method differently (Label instead of label) so the parent's version runs
@Override catches this - add it and Java will complain if the names do not match
Writes if (p is Drink) checks inside the loop
Let each object answer for itself - that is the whole point of polymorphism

weeks.title: Interfaces: The Promo Promise
weeks.goal: I can write an interface as a promise of abilities and have different classes keep that promise in their own way.
weeks.learn: An interface is a list of abilities a class promises to have, without saying how. Discountable promises 'I can give a discounted price'; Perishable promises 'I can tell you if I expire soon'. A class uses implements to keep the promise, and one class can keep many promises. It is like the badges on a POS agent's stand: 'Transfers here', 'Airtime here' - each badge is a promise, and each agent delivers it their own way.

research.q: Ask a shop owner: which of your goods can go on promo, and which ones can spoil quickly?
research.tip: Make two lists. Items on both lists are like our Bread: they implement two interfaces.

build.task: Create Discountable and Perishable interfaces, make Bread implement both and Soap implement one, then run a 20% promo.
steps: Save as Promo.java, compile and run
Change the discount from 20 to 10
Make a new class (e.g. Tomatoes) implement both interfaces
Add it to the promo array

check.q: What is an interface in Java?
opts: A list of abilities a class promises to have

check.q: Which keyword makes a class keep an interface's promise?
Can one class implement two interfaces?
opts: Yes, like Bread implements Discountable and Perishable

weeks.say: An interface is a promise like a POS badge, and each class that implements it keeps the promise in its own way.

trainer.open: Look at any POS stand: the badges tell you what they can do. In Java, those badges are called interfaces.
plan: Show pictures or drawings of POS stand badges and ask what each promises
Write the two interfaces and explain implements
Pairs run Promo and add a new class from their research
Discuss: when would you use an interface instead of inheritance?
lookfor: Explains an interface as a promise, not a pattern
Implements every method the interface lists
Places items from research in the right interfaces
fix: Forgets public on the method and gets 'attempting to assign weaker access privileges'
Interface methods are public promises - write public before them in the class
Implements an interface but leaves out one method
A promise must be kept fully - Java will name the missing method in the error

weeks.title: Try and Catch: When the Shop Boy Types 'five'
weeks.goal: I can use try/catch to stop bad input from crashing my Java program and give a friendly message instead.
weeks.learn: An exception is Java's way of saying 'something went wrong here'. Without help, the program crashes and stops. With try { } you attempt the risky line, and with catch you handle the problem calmly, then carry on. Integer.parseInt("five") throws a NumberFormatException, and dividing by zero throws an ArithmeticException. It is like NEPA taking light: a good shop has a lamp ready, so selling continues instead of closing.

research.q: Ask someone who uses a POS or a shop app: what happens when you type a wrong number? Does the app help you or confuse you?
research.tip: Write what the app said. Friendly error messages are a big part of good software.

build.task: Read four typed quantities, skip the bad ones with a friendly message, and total only the good ones.
steps: Save as SafeQty.java, compile and run
Notice the program does not crash on "five" or "0"
Add a new typed value like "-3" and think: should that be allowed?
Write a friendlier message in the catch

check.q: What happens to a Java program when an exception is NOT caught?
Which exception does Integer.parseInt("five") throw?
Why is total still correct after the bad inputs?
opts: Because the bad lines were caught before total += qty ran

weeks.say: try/catch is my NEPA lamp: when something goes wrong, my program handles it kindly and keeps selling.

trainer.open: Real people type wrong things all the time. Today we stop one wrong letter from shutting down the whole shop.
plan: Show a crash first: run Integer.parseInt("five") without try
Add try/catch step by step on the projector
Pairs run SafeQty and add their own bad inputs
Share the error messages from their research and rewrite one to be friendlier
props: A rechargeable lamp or torch for the NEPA analogy
lookfor: Predicts which input causes which exception
Explains why total skips bad lines
Writes a clear, kind error message
fix: Wraps the whole program in one try and catches Exception, hiding every problem
Catch the specific exceptions you expect, close to the risky line, so you know what went wrong
Leaves the catch block empty
An empty catch is like a lamp with no battery - always tell the user what happened

weeks.title: Throw Your Own: OutOfStockException
weeks.goal: I can create my own exception, throw it when a rule is broken, and use finally for a step that must always happen.
weeks.learn: Java lets you invent exceptions for your own business rules. OutOfStockException is thrown with throw when a customer asks for more than the shop has. The method warns callers with throws, and the caller must catch it. finally runs every time, problem or not, like a cashier who writes in the daily book after every customer whether they bought or not.

research.q: Ask a shop owner: what do you say to a customer when you do not have enough of what they want?
research.tip: Write their exact words. Put them in your exception message so the program speaks like a real trader.

build.task: Make an OutOfStockException and throw it when an order is bigger than the milk in stock.
steps: Save as Sell.java, compile and run
Follow the three orders: which one fails and why?
Put your research words into the exception message
Change the orders so two of them fail

check.q: Which keyword actually raises your own exception?
When does the finally block run?
opts: Only when there is an error

check.q: Why does the order for 4 fail?
opts: Only 3 tins were left after the first sale

weeks.say: I made my own OutOfStockException, threw it when a rule was broken, and finally always wrote in the daily book.

trainer.open: A good trader never just goes silent when stock runs out. Today your program learns to say 'Sorry o' properly.
plan: Act it out: a 'shop' with 5 bottle caps and three customers asking for 2, 4 and 3
Show the new exception class, throw, throws and finally
Pairs run Sell and trace the milk count on paper
Pairs change the message to their trader's words
props: A small notebook as the 'daily book'
lookfor: Traces the milk count after each order correctly
Explains throw vs throws
Says why finally is useful (records, closing files)
fix: Forgets 'throws OutOfStockException' on the method and gets 'unreported exception'
Java wants a warning sign on the method - add throws so callers know to catch it
Thinks finally only runs when there is an error
Watch the output: the daily-book line prints after EVERY order

weeks.title: Save It: Writing Stock to a File
weeks.goal: I can write a shop's stock list to a text file in Java and handle the IOException safely.
weeks.learn: Variables disappear when the program closes, like chalk on a board after rain. Files keep data safe. PrintWriter with FileWriter writes lines to a file, and try-with-resources (the brackets after try) closes the file automatically. Writing can fail, for example if the disk is full, so Java makes you catch IOException. We save each item as name,quantity,price - one product per line, called CSV.

research.q: Ask a shop owner: how do you keep your stock records today - a notebook, a phone, or in your head? What happens if it gets lost?
research.tip: Write their answer. If records get lost, your file-saving program is solving a real problem.

build.task: Save four provision items with quantities and prices into stock.txt.
steps: Save as SaveStock.java, compile and run
Open stock.txt in a text editor to see the lines
Add an item from your research to all three arrays
Run again and check the file updated

check.q: Why save data to a file?
opts: Variables vanish when the program closes; files keep data

check.q: What does try-with-resources (the brackets after try) do?
In our file, what does the line Garri,25,800 mean?
opts: Item Garri, 25 in stock, N800 each

weeks.say: My program saves the stock list in a file so it is not lost like chalk in the rain, and it catches IOException safely.

trainer.open: If the shop's notebook falls in a gutter, the records are gone. Today we give the shop a notebook that cannot get wet.
plan: Write a price on the board, wipe it off: 'that is a variable when the program ends'
Pairs run SaveStock and open stock.txt
Pairs add their research items and check the file
props: A wet or torn notebook page
lookfor: Opens the file and reads a line in plain words
Keeps the three arrays the same length
Explains why IOException must be caught
fix: Adds an item to items but not to qty and price, then gets ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
The three arrays are three columns of one table - every row needs all three
Cannot find stock.txt
It is saved in the folder you ran java from - check that folder

weeks.title: Project: Read the Stock, Find the Gaps
weeks.goal: I can read the stock file back into Java, total the shop's stock value and list items that need restocking.
weeks.learn: BufferedReader reads a file one line at a time, and readLine() gives null when the file ends. split(",") cuts each line into pieces, and Integer.parseInt turns text back into numbers. We catch IOException in case the file is missing and NumberFormatException in case a line is broken. Together with last week, this is a real inventory manager: save at closing time, read at opening time, like a shop that counts its goods every morning.

research.q: Ask a shop owner: every morning, what do you need to know first about your stock?
research.tip: Write their answer. Make your program's first printed line answer exactly that question.

build.task: Read stock.txt, print a restock warning for items under 10, and print the total stock value.
steps: Run last week's SaveStock first so stock.txt exists
Save this as ReadStock.java, compile and run
Open stock.txt, break one line on purpose (e.g. Rice,abc,1200) and run again
Change the restock rule to your shop owner's number

check.q: What does readLine() return when the file has no more lines?
What does line.split(",") do to "Sugar,8,1100"?
Which exception is caught if stock.txt is missing?

weeks.say: My inventory manager reads the stock file line by line, warns about low items and totals the value, without crashing on bad lines.

trainer.open: Last week we saved the shop's records. Today the shop opens, and our program tells the owner what she needs to know first.
plan: Recap: save at closing, read at opening

Pairs run ReadStock, then break a line on purpose to test the catch
Pairs present their inventory manager to a 'shop owner' (a classmate)

Uses parts[0] as the quantity
Count from 0: parts[0] is the name, parts[1] the quantity, parts[2] the price
